questions.text: Why are missing values problematic for machine learning models?
options: They make the dataset look incomplete
Most ML algorithms cannot process missing values directly
They always indicate data collection errors
They reduce the file size of the dataset
questions.explanation: Most machine learning algorithms cannot handle missing values directly and will either throw errors or produce incorrect results. Missing values must be handled before training models.

questions.text: Which imputation method replaces missing values with the average of non-missing values?
questions.explanation: Mean imputation replaces missing values with the arithmetic mean (average) of all non-missing values in that feature.

questions.text: Median imputation is more robust to outliers than mean imputation.
questions.explanation: True. The median is less affected by extreme values (outliers) than the mean, making median imputation more robust when outliers are present in the data.

questions.text: Which imputation method is most appropriate for time series data?
questions.explanation: Forward fill is most appropriate for time series data because it preserves temporal patterns by using the last observed value. This makes sense when values change slowly over time.

questions.text: What does MCAR stand for in the context of missing data?
questions.explanation: MCAR stands for Missing Completely At Random, which means the missing values are unrelated to any observed or unobserved data. This is the best-case scenario for missing data.

questions.text: What is a major disadvantage of mean/median imputation?
options: It only works for categorical data
It reduces the variance in the data
questions.explanation: A major disadvantage of mean/median imputation is that it reduces variance in the data because all imputed values are the same (the mean or median). This can distort relationships between features and affect model performance.

questions.text: Mode imputation is most suitable for which type of data?
questions.explanation: Mode imputation (using the most frequent value) is most suitable for categorical or discrete data where the concept of 'most common' is meaningful. It's not ideal for continuous numerical data with many unique values.
